content: The Oregon University System wants to update the Get Real website to encourage high-school students to consider computer science degrees and careers. The site should provide a teen-friendly path through university course information, career guidance, stories from computing professionals, and practical preparation advice. It should serve both students already interested in computing and college-bound students who may need more context or encouragement.

At the biggest picture, we want the site to help students see computer science as something they can actually belong in, not just as an abstract subject or a field for “other people.” It should build interest, reduce intimidation, and give them a clearer sense of whether this path fits their strengths, goals, and lifestyle.
That means the site should help them answer practical questions like what computer science is really like, what kinds of careers it can lead to, what classes they should take now, and what they need to do to prepare for college. It should also help them decide whether they want to keep exploring, start planning seriously, or just get enough context to feel more open to the idea.

I’d expect the content to be created by whoever is closest to the material, so probably a mix of university web people, faculty or department staff, and maybe someone who understands student outreach and teen-friendly language. Anything about careers or preparation would need review from subject matter experts so we don’t oversimplify or accidentally give wrong advice.
In practice, I’d want a draft-review-approval flow with one person owning each page, then a content review from the academic side, and a final signoff from the project lead or communications lead before publishing. If there are student stories or quotes, those would also need extra review for accuracy and permissions.

We definitely need to account for accessibility standards, so the site should be written clearly and structured in a way that works well with screen readers, keyboard navigation, and mobile devices. Since this is for a university system, the content also needs to stay consistent with institutional branding and any policies around student communications and public web content.
Legally, I’d be careful about claims that sound like guarantees, especially around careers, admissions, or outcomes, and I’d want any student photos, stories, or quotes handled with proper consent. I’m not aware of any content that would need to be restricted for different audiences, but if we include anything that’s more detailed or sensitive, that would probably need a review step and maybe a different publishing process.

Ideally, very little, if any, personal data from casual visitors. If we do collect anything, it would probably just be basic contact information for students who choose to ask for more information, sign up for updates, or request to be connected with someone.
I’d want us to be very careful about asking teens for more than we need, and I’m not sure we’d need any sensitive data at all. If we do collect it, it should be clearly explained and tied to a specific student action, not gathered by default.

Students need enough detail to understand what they’d actually be signing up for, but not so much that it feels like a catalog dump. I’d want the site to explain what the major or program focuses on, what kinds of classes come early versus later, what skills or interests fit well, and where that path can lead after graduation.
That information should help them compare options and figure out their next step, like whether they should explore an introductory course, look at a specific campus, or read more about a related career. If possible, it should also make clear which programs are good for beginners and which ones assume they already have some background.

The authoritative source should be the official university catalog or the registrar-approved course system, since that’s what students and advisors can rely on. If the website ever shows something different, the site should defer to the official source and make that clear rather than trying to interpret it on its own.
If the information seems out of date or conflicts across systems, I’d want the site to either hide the questionable detail or mark it as needing verification until someone confirms it. We definitely don’t want to send students down the wrong path based on stale prerequisites or a description that has changed.

It should feel welcoming, simple, and not too academic right away. A teen should immediately understand that this is a place to explore computer science in a low-pressure way, with a few clear choices like learning what CS is, hearing from real people, or finding out how to prepare.
I’d want the first screen to avoid clutter and jargon, and to guide them toward one or two obvious next steps instead of a lot of competing links. The overall feeling should be, “you can start here even if you’re just curious,” and then the site can gradually give them more detail as they choose to dig deeper.

It should work very well on phones, since a lot of teens will probably find it that way first. The important thing is that the main next steps stay obvious even on a small screen, and that pages still load quickly if the connection is slow.
I’d also want the layout to stay clean and easy to tap, with no tiny text or buried menus that make it hard to keep going. If something is heavy, like a video or image, the site should still give them a usable path without making them wait.

The main journeys that need to carry over are the ones that help a student go from curiosity to action, like learning what computer science is, finding related university programs, reading student or professional stories, and figuring out how to prepare. If there’s already content that helps with those steps, it should not get lost in the move.
I think the old content should probably be reorganized around those student goals rather than copied over as-is, and anything outdated or redundant should be cleaned up. If some pages are still useful but don’t fit the new flow, they can be kept as supporting content, but the new structure should make the path much clearer.

We should preserve as much of that traffic as possible by redirecting old URLs to the most relevant new pages. If a page still exists in a new form, the old link should take people straight there so bookmarks and search results don’t break.
If a page no longer has a good replacement, then I’d still want a clear fallback rather than a dead end, probably something that explains the page moved and points them to the closest useful section. The main goal is to avoid confusing students or losing people who are already trying to get to us.

Anything that is official university information needs to be tightly controlled, especially course descriptions, prerequisites, program requirements, and any content that could affect advising decisions. I’d also be careful with student stories, photos, and any personal information, since those need proper permission and review.
As for publishing, I’d expect only authorized staff to be able to update those sections, with some kind of review before anything goes live. We don’t want random edits or uncaptured changes, because that could create compliance problems or give students the wrong impression.

I don’t have a specific CMS name decided already. What matters to us is that it’s easy for staff to update, supports approvals or workflow, and can handle media and redirects cleanly.
If there’s a platform that already fits with the university’s existing environment, that would probably be the first thing to consider. Otherwise, we’d need to choose something that doesn’t make publishing harder for non-technical staff.

Those changes need to be reflected quickly and consistently, because students may be relying on them to plan their next steps. I’d want the site to show the current official version, and if something changes mid-term, it should be clear that the information has been updated.
If possible, it would also help to keep a record of what changed and when, just for accountability. We don’t necessarily need to expose the whole history to students, but the team should be able to verify what was published if there’s ever a question.

Once it’s approved, the new version should go live in a way that replaces the old official information right away, so students always see the current content. I’d also want the system to keep a simple internal audit trail with the date, time, who made the change, and what was changed.
It doesn’t need to be complicated for the public, but internally we should be able to verify that the right version was published and when it happened. That would help if anyone later asks why something looked different or when the change took effect.

Yes, there are probably a few exceptions, especially for urgent fixes or time-sensitive notices. If something is clearly wrong, like a typo in a prerequisite or a broken link, that shouldn’t have to wait through a long review.
For emergency or very short-timeline updates, I’d expect a faster approval path with the same general accountability, so the content can be corrected quickly without losing track of who changed it and why.

In general, content creation and editing should be limited to the people responsible for that area, like the communications team or the academic unit that owns the information. Final approval should sit with the appropriate university authority for that content, usually someone in the program or department who can confirm it’s accurate and official.
For especially sensitive material, I’d want a second set of eyes before it goes live, but I don’t think every small update needs a big committee-style process.

We should definitely capture accessibility and branding requirements now, because those are core expectations for a public university site. Accessibility should meet the university’s standards, and branding should stay consistent with the rest of Oregon University System materials.
Any detailed compliance rules beyond that can probably be left a bit open for now if they’re not fully settled, but I wouldn’t mark the whole area as undecided.

They should get a basic onboarding session on how to create, edit, and publish content in the new system, plus a short guide they can refer back to later. I’d also want some training on writing for high school students, accessibility basics, and how to keep the tone and visuals aligned with the brand.
After launch, there should be a clear support contact or help channel so editors can get answers quickly when they’re unsure.

They should have a clear escalation path, so they know exactly who to contact for each kind of issue rather than guessing. If it’s accessibility, branding, or legal, I’d expect them to route it to the designated expert or reviewer and hold the content until they get an answer.
If the question is blocking publication and there’s a deadline, the support process should be responsive enough to turn things around quickly, but still preserve the approval trail.

They usually hesitate when the site gets too technical too quickly, like when we jump straight into course requirements or jargon without first explaining what computer science actually is. Another common drop-off point is when they can’t tell whether a degree is for them, so they start doubting if they belong or if it’s too hard.
Confusion also happens when information feels disconnected, like they can’t easily move from “I’m curious” to “what should I take in high school” to “what careers does this lead to.”

We should feature a broad mix, not just software developers. It would help to include people in areas like cybersecurity, data science, systems or network administration, game development, user experience, and maybe someone who works in tech support or IT and moved into a more specialized role.
It would also be good to show a range of backgrounds and paths, including students who started unsure, transfer students, and professionals who came to computing from something nontraditional.

Yes, I’d keep the stories tied to a clear purpose in the student journey. For example, if we feature someone with an unusual path, it should help explain that there isn’t just one way into computer science, or it should address a specific concern like math anxiety, not just be interesting on its own.
I’d avoid stories that feel too advanced, too niche, or too insider-focused, because high school students may not see themselves in them. The goal is to make the path feel possible and relatable, not to showcase the most impressive or technical story available.

Yes, definitely. It would be useful to show moments where they weren’t sure about the major, switched directions, found computing later than expected, or needed encouragement before they felt confident. That helps students see that uncertainty is normal and that you don’t have to have a perfect plan at the start.
We’d also want the story to show a turning point, like a class, mentor, project, or internship that made computing feel real and doable.

For students who already like computing, the stories can go a little deeper into the work itself and the different specializations, because they’re looking for ways to narrow things down. For students who are unsure or intimidated, the stories should be more about relatability, confidence-building, and showing how someone got started without being an expert right away.
In both cases, the story should still feel practical and grounded, but the emphasis changes depending on whether we’re trying to spark interest or help them picture a next step.

The primary audience is students who are college-bound but not necessarily set on computer science yet. We want the site to speak first to the ones who are curious, undecided, or a little unsure whether this field is for them, because they need the most context and encouragement.
The students who already know they like computing are still important, but the main message should be broad and welcoming so it doesn’t assume prior confidence or knowledge.

I’d aim it first at high school students in about grades 9 through 12, with a strong focus on juniors and seniors who are starting to think seriously about college choices. That said, the tone should still be accessible enough for younger students who are just beginning to explore what computer science even is.
The site should not feel like it’s written for college students or professionals. It needs to meet high schoolers where they are and help them imagine a path forward.

It should start with simple, friendly language and a very clear sense of where to begin, rather than a lot of detailed course or career information right away. Early on, I’d want it to explain what computer science is in plain terms, show a few relatable examples, and give them easy choices instead of making them read a lot before they can move on.
It would also help to reassure them that they do not need to know everything yet. The first few minutes should feel welcoming and low-pressure, like the site is guiding them rather than testing them.

They should have a clear point of contact and some simple editorial guidance they can rely on after launch, because those issues will come up quickly. I’d want help with things like keeping the tone teen-friendly, checking accessibility, and deciding whether a new story or page fits the audience before it goes live.
If there’s a problem they can’t resolve on their own, the process should be straightforward so they know who to ask and how quickly they’ll get an answer.

In practice, I’d expect the content editor or site manager to be the one who requests the change, and then at least one reviewer with authority over the program content should sign off before it goes live. Anything that looks official, like course details, advising guidance, deadlines, or links to university resources, should probably need an extra check from the owning department or a designated approver.
We’d want the process to be simple enough that updates don’t get stuck, but strict enough that we don’t publish something inaccurate or inconsistent with the universities’ official information.

I’d put things like interactive quizzes, personalized recommendations, video-heavy storytelling, and more advanced filtering into later phases if we need to keep the first release focused. Those would be great additions, but they’re not as important as getting the core guidance, stories, and practical information right first.
I’d pull a feature into the first release only if it clearly helps a student understand the path into computer science or removes a major barrier to using the site. If it’s mostly extra engagement, it can wait.

They should be able to jump straight to the most relevant section. We still want the site to connect the dots across curiosity, preparation, and careers, but it shouldn’t force everyone through the full sequence if they already know what they’re looking for.
At the same time, each section should make it easy to explore the next step if they want it, so they can move forward naturally without feeling trapped in one path.

I’d group courses in a way that feels intuitive to a high school student, so broad themes would probably be the main approach, with optional career-related tags where that helps explain why a course matters. If a course clearly fits more than one area, I’d expect it to appear in more than one group rather than forcing it into just one.
I’d leave a course out of the grouping only if it’s too specialized or if we can’t describe it in a way that makes sense to that audience without confusing them.

I’d prefer one primary placement with links or references from the other groups, so we don’t create a lot of duplicate content for students to read through. That keeps the experience cleaner and makes it easier to maintain if the course description changes later.
If a student finds the course from a secondary group, it should still feel like a direct path to the same information, just without repeating everything in full.

In most cases, every entry should point students to the same course page so the core information stays consistent. The secondary listings could have a slightly different label or short note to explain why the course appears there, but I wouldn’t want the underlying details or calls to action to drift from one listing to another.
If we do vary anything, it should be minimal and only for orientation, not for changing the meaning of the course itself.

We should be careful to present examples as examples, not promises. So if we show a student story or a graduate outcome, it should be framed as one person’s path or one possible result, and we should avoid language that suggests everyone who follows this path will get the same career or admission outcome.
At the same time, the content can still be persuasive by being specific about skills, preparation, and opportunities, just without making guarantees. A clear tone like “this can lead to” or “students may explore” feels safer and still useful.

Yes, definitely. If a story is unusual, still in progress, or depends on a very specific opportunity, I’d want that made clear right in the story so students don’t assume it’s the normal path.
Even for more typical stories, a light qualifier can help, but we especially need it when the example could be mistaken for a guarantee or a standard outcome.

Yes, there are limits, but I’d want legal and institutional review before we lock down exact wording. In general, we should avoid absolute claims like guaranteed job placement, guaranteed admission, or “everyone can do this if they try,” because those can be misleading and hard to defend.
If a story or outcome is sensitive, we should add a plain-language disclosure that it’s an example, not a promise, and make sure any wording is accessible and easy to understand for teens and families.

I’d expect final wording to go through whoever owns the site content on the university side, plus communications or marketing, and legal review for anything that sounds like an outcome claim, student promise, or endorsement. If there’s accessibility language, privacy concerns, or a featured person’s personal story, I’d want those checked too before anything goes live.
Anything that could be read as a guarantee, a recruitment promise, or a sensitive personal statement should be escalated. If we’re unsure whether a claim is too strong, it’s better to route it for review than to publish first and fix later.

Yes, probably. I don’t have the exact staffing or budget numbers yet, but if review cycles are slow or the team is small, we may need to batch updates, simplify approvals, or hold some content until it can be properly checked.
I’d rather do fewer updates well than push out a lot of changes that haven’t been reviewed.

Yes, compatibility should be a priority, because we don’t want the new site to create extra work for the university team. The biggest things are whether the CMS fits the current hosting and security environment, works with existing user login or permission setups if needed, and can support the university’s design and accessibility standards.
It would also help if it integrates cleanly with any existing analytics, media hosting, or course information sources we already rely on.

It needs to fit a fairly standard university environment, so secure hosting, regular updates, and role-based access control are important. If we use identity management, it should work with the university’s existing sign-in approach rather than creating a separate one for staff.
It also needs to support analytics we can use for site improvement, and it should be able to pull in or link to existing content sources without a lot of manual re-entry. I don’t know yet if there are any environments we must avoid, but anything that’s hard to secure, hard to maintain, or difficult to make accessible would be a concern.

I don’t know the specific identity provider offhand, and I’d need to confirm that with the university IT team. My assumption is that it should work with whatever the university already uses for staff single sign-on, rather than asking staff to manage a separate CMS account system.
If there are multiple campuses or units involved, we should verify whether they all use the same sign-in method or if there are exceptions.

We’d want the site to support basic usage analytics, like page visits, where users enter and leave, and which course or career pages get the most attention. It would also be useful to see whether teens are finding the practical prep content, stories, and degree information, since that tells us if the path through the site is working.
I don’t know yet if there are specific formal reports the university expects, but audience insights like school-aged visitors versus adult visitors, and what content leads people deeper into the site, would be especially helpful.

The most useful breakdowns would probably be by entry page, referral source, and the path people take through the site before reaching course or career pages. If we can separate likely high-school visitors from older audiences in some reasonable way, that would help too, even if it’s only approximate.
It would also be valuable to see which sequences work best, like whether students come in through a story, then move to what to study, then to career guidance. That kind of flow would tell us what content is actually helping them along.

Success would mostly mean a visitor gets from the teen-friendly intro content into the more substantive course or career information, and spends enough time there to actually engage with it. If they also move on to related pages like preparation advice or stories, that’s a good sign the site is helping them explore.
A weaker path would be one where people arrive, bounce quickly, or stop at a general page without getting to anything that explains why computer science might matter to them. We are not necessarily expecting an application or sign-up action right away, since this site is more about interest and guidance.

For routine changes, I’d expect a contributor or content owner to draft them and an approver to review before anything goes live. Small edits like typo fixes or a quick update to a date might be able to move faster, but only if they’re low risk and still follow whatever authorization the university requires.
For time-sensitive items, such as a deadline or event change, we’d want a clear expedited path so it doesn’t get stuck, but I don’t know yet exactly who can bypass normal review. That would need to be defined carefully so we don’t trade speed for mistakes.

I’d use impact and urgency as the main filters. If a change affects deadlines, broken links, inaccurate course information, or something a student could act on right away, it should move faster; if it’s just a polish item or a minor wording improvement, it can wait for the next batch.
If staffing is tight, we should bundle non-urgent updates into scheduled review windows so the team isn’t constantly interrupting its work. Anything that is low value, duplicative, or likely to change again soon should probably be deferred rather than churned through the process.

I’d treat it as truly urgent if delaying it would mislead students, cause them to miss an important deadline, or leave them with broken or outdated information that affects their next step. Things like a changed course offering, an admissions deadline, or a correction to a serious factual error would fit that.
If it’s just helpful to have sooner, but not harmful to wait, then it can stay in the normal batch. The main test is whether the delay creates real student impact or just a little inconvenience.

Usually that should be limited to the content owner or a designated approver, and only for clearly defined urgent cases. I’d want them to have enough authority to act quickly, but not so much that they can bypass review for routine changes.
For that to happen, the update would need to be genuinely time-sensitive, low risk to the site’s accuracy or tone, and ideally documented so the normal reviewers know what changed afterward. If there’s any chance it could confuse students or affect important guidance, I’d rather it still go through review.

The site should make coursework and skills learned the clearest, because those are the things students can most directly understand and compare. Career outcomes are important too, especially for showing what kinds of jobs each path can lead to, but I’d keep that tied to real examples rather than abstract claims.
Admissions fit matters as well, but more as practical guidance than as a comparison chart. The main goal is to help a student see which path feels right for them and what it actually takes to get there.

Yes, definitely. They should be coached to write at a high school reading level, use plain vocabulary, and explain any technical terms instead of assuming students already know them. Examples should feel real and relatable, like school projects, apps, games, or everyday problem solving.
They should also avoid jargon, overly academic tone, and anything that sounds like marketing fluff. I’d want them to be careful not to be condescending either, since the audience ranges from curious students to those who may need a lot more reassurance.

We’d want to avoid anything that makes the site hard to secure or maintain, especially if it creates extra steps every time someone updates content. Security review should be built into the environment, and accessibility support needs to be consistent rather than optional, since this is a public university site.
If the CMS pulls content from other systems, like course or admissions data, it should do that in a controlled way so we’re not manually duplicating information. Sign-in integration is probably only needed for editors and approvers, not for students browsing the site, but I’d want that confirmed with the technical team.

They should have a clear path to a site owner or content lead first, and if it’s accessibility-related, there should also be a designated accessibility contact or reviewer. I’d expect routine questions to get a response within a few business days, but if it blocks a publish or affects a deadline, it should escalate faster.
If the first contact can’t resolve it, it should move to whoever has final approval authority for that area. The important thing is that people know who to ask and aren’t left guessing while an issue sits unresolved.

If the final approver is unavailable, it should be reassigned to a backup approver so the work doesn’t just stall. If they disagree, I’d want the issue documented and either sent to a higher-level owner or brought back with clear guidance on what needs to change.
The key is that there should be a fallback path, because some updates are time-sensitive and we can’t have them stuck waiting on one person.

If it can’t meet the expected standard, it should generally block publication until the issue is fixed. If there’s a rare case where something has to go live, I’d only want a temporary exception with documented review, a clear reason, and a plan to correct it quickly.
I wouldn’t want exceptions to become the norm, because this site needs to be usable for everyone from the start.

Yes, I think it depends on the type of issue and how urgent it is. If it’s just an availability issue, it should be reassigned to a backup approver; if there’s a disagreement, it should go back with specific required changes unless it’s something that really needs a policy-level decision.
Only the bigger or more sensitive cases should escalate to a higher-level owner, especially if the content affects compliance, accessibility, or a major public-facing deadline.

Escalation should happen when the issue changes more than just wording or small content details, especially if it affects accessibility compliance, legal sensitivity, or whether the page can publish on time. If it’s something the editor or backup can reasonably fix with clear comments, then it should just go back for revision.
I’d also escalate if the approver and contributor are stuck in a loop and there’s no path to resolution without a higher-level judgment.

Yes, there could be cases where a secondary group needs its own short explanation if the course plays a different role there, like showing how it fits a pathway or a career interest. But in general, I’d still want the primary placement to be the main source of truth, and secondary placements should usually just point back there.
If there’s a real difference in audience or context, then a fuller summary or a different link makes sense, but we’d want to keep that limited so it doesn’t create conflicting information.

Yes, I think we’d want to separate some of that by audience and context, especially if the needs are different enough that the messaging or next step changes. For example, a high-school student looking for encouragement should probably see a different path than a parent, counselor, or older visitor who’s just looking for factual details.
At the same time, if two entry sources lead to the same kind of intent, it’s fine to group them together. The main thing is that the grouping should help us tailor the experience, not just create segments for the sake of it.

The biggest cue is probably the entry point itself, like whether they came in through a student-facing page, a career story, or something more informational like course details. Age isn’t always obvious, so we’d rely more on the kind of content they’re already looking at and whether they seem to need encouragement versus straight facts.
If someone is on a page about getting started, we should keep the tone friendly and simple, while a page for course planning can use a bit more precise terminology. If we can’t tell, I’d rather default to clear and approachable language so we don’t lose anybody.
